The Snake River. Flowing approximately one thousand forty miles through the Pacific Northwest, the Snake originates in the Teton Range of Wyoming and flows westward through Idaho before joining the Columbia River in Washington. It is the Columbia's largest tributary and drains a vast plateau region of the American interior West. The river originates near Jackson Lake in the Teton Range on the Wyoming-Idaho border and flows through mountains before continuing across the Snake River Plain. The name comes from the distinctive S-shaped bends along portions of its course, though some sources attribute it to a Shoshone or Nez Perce word. The river flows westward across Idaho, carving the Hells Canyon, a dramatic seven-thousand-foot gorge that is among North America's deepest river canyons. It is extensively dammed with multiple hydroelectric projects including the Brownlee, Oxbow, and Hells Canyon Dams, primarily for power generation and irrigation purposes. The Snake joins the Columbia River in Washington, and this union dramatically increases the Columbia's volume and power. The river was historically crucial for fur trading and exploration in the Pacific Northwest, followed by trappers and early settlement throughout the region. It supports a complex ecosystem and fishery, though dam construction has significantly impacted salmon populations and ecological integrity. The river remains a vital waterway connecting the interior plateau to the Pacific Northwest.
